Had this the other night, nicest roast ever (and I've had my fair share), so I'll share the recipe. No photo - I don't know if that's a requirement. Perhaps some keen soul can do it and post a shot. I devoured mine then thought, good lord, this is worthy of an internet posting. Nice bit of beef helps too I guess as the cooking time seems short (I prefer to go slow and low).

  1. Mix these:

    • 90g or 1/3 cup of Dijon mustard
    • 2 tablespoons soy sauce
    • 2 tablespoons olive oil
    • 2 tablespoons flour (plain, not self-raising)
    • 2 teaspoons of chopped thyme (fresh if possible, I guess perhaps 1 of dried)
    • 2 crushed garlic cloves (don't use that jar nonsense, its foul)
    • 1 tablespoon cracked fresh black pepper

  2. Coat a roast of beef in the above, recipe calls for 2.5kg but whatever you have. Once coated, put it on a rack in the fridge for 1 hr and the coating will firm up.

  3. Recipe calls for hasselback spuds, which are essentially par-boiled, sliced 2/3 of the way through and a bit of butter rubbed in and baked, but that's a trivial part, roast veges are a no brainer ... the roast beef is the important bit. So time whatever veges (parsnips are my go to, as are spuds, celery and pumpkin) base on the latter.

  4. The sauce part is:

    • 1/4 cup of olive oil (minus the two tablespoons you used above). Heat that in a pan
    • Add 1 roughly copped onion (not too rough), 1 large carrot (again diced), 2 celery stalks (chopped), 2 garlic cloves crushed up.
    • Cook that for 5 minutes, let the aroma drive you wild
    • Pour in 1 cup of red wine (I used a cab sav, but something nice and drinkable)
    • Cook for a further 5 minutes
      • Add 2 cups of a good beef stock, 2 bay leaves and 1 teaspoon of thyme
    • Mix 2 teaspoons of cornflour and 1 tablespoon of water, throw that in
    • Simmer on low for 20 minutes or until thickened a bit, then strain. and then season with salt/pepper

  5. In parallel, be cooking the roast. The recipe calls for a BBQ for 45 minutes. You can use a meat thermo to get it to how you like it, or do the beef first really slow and low for 4 hours and at the last minute scorch it etc.

  6. Rest roast, carve it very thinly, serve with the sauce and hassleback spuds, asparagus, newborn pugs, and possibly a nice salad/vinagerraitesae.
Roast Sirloin with Mustard Pepper Crust and Hasselback Potatoes

I also quickly made some bonus questions for any keen basketball nerds. The questions will be left in the comments. What is a backdoor cut? A backdoor cut is an offensive move whereby an off-ball player looks to cut to the basket behind the defense. As a player, the first shots you should learn to make are layups, and backdoor cuts are a great way to get yourself plenty of layups.

<h1>Pattern No.1: Overly-aggresive defense</h1>

Many people will tell you that defense is all about effort. If this were true, then being as aggressive as possible would always lead to success on defense. Unfortunately, defense is not so simple and aggressive defense is not always the smart option.

Image

If we firstly look at wing passes, we see the issue caused by aggressive off-ball defense: although the space in front of player 2 is covered, the defender has now left a huge hole behind him (the space behind the red line in the above image). The offensive player can look to exploit this with a backdoor cut.

Here we see Jimmy Butler doing this in his playoff series against the Bucks

Now, we see that there are two tidbits of information to keep in mind:

1. The defender’s speed vs the offensive player’s speed. The defender is essentially giving the offensive player a headstart in the race to the basket. This headstart won’t be significant if the defender is much faster than his man.

2. Spacing. In the first diagram, I only showed a 2 v 2 setting where both players were on the perimeter. Imagine 3 players clogging 2’s path to the basket. In this example, we see Okafor clogs the lane to the basket and this is enough to stop the play:

The second point can help us explain why backdoor cuts are so popular in one area of the court – the corner.

<h1>Backdoor cuts from the corner</h1>

NBA teams like to run a lot screens and dribble handoffs for a player in the corner to curl towards the top of the key. Here we see a typical action involving LeBron James.

Why is this dangerous? This naturally curving route allows the offensive player to pick up a lot of speed and momentum as he is entering the lane. Trying to stop LeBron from slowly stumbling into the lane is hard enough, but preventing him from cutting inside while he’s running at full speed just seems impossible. There’s also the chance that they can receive the ball and take a quick jump shot. As they curl around the wing towards the top of the key, their bodies should be well aligned to the basket, meaning this option is also a serious danger.

So okay, this action is dangerous and you want to prevent this headache from occurring, so you look to deny the pass. Simple, right? Well, the problem is that the lane to the basket from the corner is often completely vacant, which leads to a lot of this.

You may notice how Kevin Durant faked the curl towards the ball to get his defender, Paul George, to go one way, before going the other way to cut backdoor. This is a great way of setting up a backdoor cut.

Also remember that the corners are much closer to the basket than anywhere else on the perimeter (such as the aforementioned wings). This means that a help defender has less time to clog the lane to the basket.

<h1>Pattern No. 2: Sneaking past the defender</h1>

The previous two patterns of play came as a result of overly-eager defense, so surely if you step back off of your man, you don’t have to worry about any backdoor cuts, right?

Well unfortunately this is not the case. If you are too busy ball watching, your man could look to exploit this by sneaking past you to the basket. A backdoor cut represents a race to the basket, but if the defender isn’t paying attention then he won’t even know that the race has started. Tobias Harris has become the master of this.

Timing and anticipation are key here; you need to make sure that when you reach the basket, your teammate will be able to make the pass to you (he won't have his back to the basket for example) and that no defender will be able to cover you in time.

Anyway, this is just another reason why you should always pay attention to the ball AND your man.

<H1>Things you can do on the offensive end to help your team use backdoor cuts:- </H1>

1. Communicate.

Sometimes your teammate may not see how a defender is playing him, or he may not know how to exploit it. A lot of younger players take aggressive defense personally and they keep trying to force their way past their man to receive the pass. Not only is this a waste of energy, but it also slows down the team’s offense as the players have to wait for you to be able to receive the pass. Help your teammates by talking to them, it will make your team better AND it will allow you to show off your knowledge.

2. Set a screen

Earlier I mentioned that quicker defenders can sometimes get away with playing aggressive off-ball defense. What should you do if your slower teammate is being denied the ball by John Wall? You can set a back screen for your teammate to give him a few extra yards. Here we see Kobe Bryant using a back screen in a play called “blind pig” during his legendary 81 point game.

3. Clear out the driving lanes for your player

If you aren’t setting a back screen, but your player is being denied the ball, you should make sure that his lanes to the basket are cleared. If you are a low-post player, make sure you post up on the opposite side of the court to your teammate who is looking to make the backdoor cut. If the pass to the left wing is being denied, look to post up on the right-hand side of the court (or set screens for players on the RHS).

Things you can do to prevent/defend backdoor cuts:-

1. Communicate.

Sometimes your teammate will have a tendency to watch the ball. If you see this happening as Tobias Harris sneaks past him, tell your teammate to keep an eye on his man.

2. Help out on cuts.

If a player has been beaten via a backdoor cut, you want to track the cutter’s run so that he can’t receive the pass. Hopefully, this will only be temporary as your teammate can then recover onto his man, and you can go back to your original man. If your teammate is too far away from his man, you may have to switch onto the cutter for the remainder of the possession. Here we see Millsap help out on Tony Allen’s cut to the basket (not a backdoor cut, but the idea is the same). He makes sure that the pass to the basket cannot be made, before returning to Randolph.

3. Mix up how you and your teammates cover your men.

If a player is aggressively denied the pass every time he’s on the perimeter, he will eventually start to make the correct backdoor cuts. If a player’s man never pays attention to him, he will eventually start to automatically make backdoor cuts. This is why it is important to always mix up your defensive coverage; your opponents will never be sure what you will do, and how they should respond.
